stem:
A well 5-day-old baby has a second 'refer' result in the right ear on the NSW SWISH automated hearing screen; the left ear passed. There is no family history of hearing loss. A diagnostic audiology appointment has been offered for next week. The parents ask whether, with one ear that passed, they can simply wait and see.

How should the result be explained?

options.label: A
options.text: It confirms permanent hearing loss in the right ear
options.explanation: A screening result cannot diagnose hearing loss. Diagnostic audiology is needed to confirm or exclude it.

options.label: B
options.text: It probably reflects birth fluid, so rescreen in three months
options.explanation: Transient causes are possible, but they cannot be assumed. Delaying diagnostic assessment delays early intervention if there is a true loss.

options.label: C
options.text: With a normal left ear, a one-sided refer needs no follow-up
options.explanation: Unilateral hearing loss can affect language and learning, so a one-sided refer still goes to diagnostic audiology.

options.label: D
options.text: It means a diagnostic assessment is needed, without confirming loss
options.explanation: A refer result identifies a baby who needs diagnostic audiology. It neither confirms nor excludes hearing loss, and the assessment should go ahead promptly even when only one ear referred.

options.label: E
options.text: It means the equipment failed, so the screen should simply be repeated
options.explanation: A refer result reflects the baby's response, not an equipment fault, and after two refer results the next step is diagnostic assessment rather than more screening.

context: A refer on newborn hearing screening, even in one ear, means prompt diagnostic audiology; it is neither a diagnosis nor something to watch.
